questions.question: What is a race condition and how do you identify one in code?
questions.title: Race Condition Identification in Java
questions.direct_answer: A race condition exists when concurrent actions on shared state can interleave and produce an incorrect result. Look for state that more than one thread can access, at least one write, and no single synchronization strategy covering the whole operation. `volatile` can make a plain value visible, but it does not make `counter++` atomic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can spot race conditions in code — practical skill for production debugging
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only describing race conditions abstractly — not being able to point to one in actual code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the exact code pattern that causes a race condition and explain the specific interleaving that breaks it

sections.title: Understanding Race Conditions in Concurrent Java
sections.content:
A **race condition** exists when a program's correctness depends on how concurrent actions happen to interleave. The usual ingredients are shared mutable state, at least one write, and no synchronization covering the complete operation.

For example, `counter++` is a read-modify-write operation. Two threads can both read 10 and both write 11, losing one update. The important point is conceptual: one Java statement is not automatically one atomic action.

To review code, first find state shared across requests or tasks. Then ask which operations must happen as one unit and what creates the required ordering: a common lock, an atomic class, an immutable design, confinement, or a suitable concurrent collection. A `volatile` counter is still unsafe for `++`; `volatile` gives visibility and ordering for that variable, not atomicity for the compound update.

sections.title: How an Interleaving Loses an Update
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Thread A reads count = 10] --> B[Thread A adds one
in a register] A2[Thread B reads count = 10] --> C2[Thread B writes 11] B --> C[Thread A writes 11] C2 --> D{Both wrote
the same 11?} C --> D D -- Yes --> E[One increment is lost] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Race Condition|~Output depends on timing|interleaved access|read-modify-write|non-deterministic
blue|Root Cause|~Shared mutable state|multiple threads write|no synchronization|unprotected section
emerald|Symptoms|~Hard to reproduce|works in dev|fails under load|flaky tests
violet|Fixes|~Make it safe|synchronized|AtomicInteger|immutability

sections.title: Wrong: an unsynchronized counter loses updates
Right: AtomicInteger makes each increment atomic
When Race Conditions Occur
sections.content:
Race conditions occur when you have **shared mutable state** accessed by multiple threads without synchronization. Common spots in a Java backend: a counter tracking requests across servlet threads, a cache map updated by concurrent API calls, or a status flag checked and changed by different workers.

You will see them most in Spring `@Service` singletons where instance fields are shared across request threads. Any time a non-final field in a singleton bean gets modified, ask: **can two threads reach this at once?** If yes, and there is no `synchronized`, `volatile`, or `AtomicX`, you have likely found a race condition waiting to happen.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming single statements are atomic**: freshers think `counter++` or `list.add()` is safe because it is one line of Java, not realizing it is not specified as one atomic action and can interleave.
- **Synchronizing only the getter**: adding `synchronized` to `getCount()` but not to `incrementCount()` does not help — both the read and the write need the same lock.
- **Relying on one test environment**: a race may stay hidden on a single-core container, then appear in production on multi-core servers where true parallelism happens.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Race condition**: correctness depends on an unsafe interleaving of concurrent actions.
- **Three clues**: shared state, at least one write, and no synchronization covering the operation.
- **`counter++`**: a read-modify-write, so two threads can lose an update.
- **`volatile` boundary**: useful for visibility of a flag, not for making `++` atomic.
- **Typical fixes**: confinement or immutability, a common lock, an atomic class, or a concurrent collection chosen for the full operation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A race condition means the result can become wrong because concurrent actions on shared data happen in an unsafe order. A simple example is a shared request counter. `counter++` reads the old value, calculates the next value, and writes it back. If two threads read 10 before either write is visible, both can write 11 and one increment is lost.

I identify a race by tracing three things: which state is shared, which code writes it, and what synchronization protects the complete operation. A non-final field in a shared service is worth checking, but the field alone is not proof of a bug; the object may be confined, immutable after publication, or protected elsewhere. The fix must match the operation. `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` fits an independent counter. A lock fits several related changes that must stay together. `volatile` alone does not fix `counter++`, because visibility is not the same as an atomic read-modify-write.

familiarity_anchors: two cashiers both ringing up the last item
two people simultaneously booking the last seat
two hands reaching for the same cookie
speakable_v2.hook: Two threads touch the same data at once. The result depends on who wins the race. That's a race condition, and it hides until production.

beats.text: A race condition is a bug where the program's output depends on thread timing. It shows up when two threads read and change the same shared data without a lock. The code looks fine. It even passes single-threaded tests. Then it fails at random under load.

The scheduler can pause any thread mid-step. A line like `count++` isn't one action. It's a read, then an add, then a write. In that gap, another thread reads the old value too. So both threads write back the same number.

items: Look for a shared mutable field touched by many threads with no lock.
Watch any read-modify-write, like incrementing a shared counter.
Watch check-then-act code, like checking stock and then placing an order.

beats.text: Picture a counter at ten. Thread A reads ten and plans eleven. Before it writes, Thread B also reads ten and writes eleven. Thread A writes eleven too. Here's the non-obvious part. You ran two increments, but the counter moved once. One update vanished, and a single-threaded test would never catch it.

items: A plain read needs a lock too. An unsynced read can see a stale value.
The fix isn't always a lock. Sometimes immutable data removes the sharing entirely.

speakable_v2.cap: So spot race conditions by finding shared mutable state and non-atomic steps. Then add a lock or remove the sharing.

questions.question: What is starvation in multithreading?
questions.title: Thread Starvation in Java
questions.direct_answer: Starvation means a thread or task is ready to make progress but keeps being denied the CPU, a lock, a pool slot, or another resource because other work is repeatedly favored. Unlike deadlock, other threads continue to make progress. Fairer scheduling or lock policies can reduce starvation, but a fair lock is not a strict guarantee of operating-system scheduling order.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the three main concurrency problems: race conditions, deadlock, and starvation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing starvation with deadlock — in starvation the thread could eventually run; in deadlock it never can
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete cause like always using notify instead of notifyAll when there are multiple waiters

sections.title: Understanding Thread Starvation
sections.content:
**Starvation** means some work is continually delayed while other work keeps making progress. The starved thread may be runnable, waiting for a lock, or queued for a limited resource; it is not limited to one Java thread state.

Common causes are long critical sections, unfair lock acquisition, thread-pool tasks that occupy every worker, or priority policies that keep favoring other work. With deadlock, a cycle prevents the involved threads from progressing. With starvation, there need not be a cycle—resources are simply allocated unfairly for a long time.

A fair `ReentrantLock` favors the longest-waiting thread when threads contend through `lock()`, which can reduce lock starvation. It does not promise strict end-to-end FIFO execution, and the operating-system scheduler can still delay a thread. The real fix is to shorten resource ownership, avoid priority dependence, bound work, and measure queue wait time.

sections.title: Why a Waiting Thread Never Gets Picked
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S[Scheduler picks next thread] --> H[High-priority thread runs] H --> S S -. never picked .-> L[Low-priority thread
ready but waiting forever] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Starvation|~Denied resource|never gets CPU/lock|others keep winning|no progress
blue|Causes|~Unfairness|greedy high-priority|always-held locks|biased scheduling
emerald|Fairness|~The remedy|fair ReentrantLock|fair Semaphore|round-robin
violet|vs Deadlock|~Different problem|starved thread could run|just never picked|not a cycle

sections.title: Wrong: notify() can leave most workers starving
Right: notifyAll() plus a fair lock prevent starvation
When Starvation Occurs
sections.content:
Starvation shows up wherever there is **resource contention and unfair allocation**. In thread pools, some tasks keep getting picked while others wait indefinitely. In producer-consumer code, using `notify()` with several consumers can leave some of them asleep forever.

Lock starvation happens with the default (unfair) `ReentrantLock` when one thread keeps re-acquiring under heavy contention. Database connection pools can starve threads if connections are not released fairly. The tell-tale sign: some threads make progress while others **with the same priority** stay blocked despite being ready to run.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing starvation with deadlock**: in deadlock, threads can never proceed; in starvation, a thread *could* run but keeps getting deprioritized.
- **Using `notify()` instead of `notifyAll()`**: the classic cause — freshers think `notify()` is more efficient, not realizing it can leave threads starving.
- **Assuming the JVM scheduler is fair**: same-priority threads may not get equal time, so you need an fair `ReentrantLock` to favor queued contenders, while remembering it is not a strict scheduler FIFO guarantee.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Starvation**: one thread or task waits indefinitely while other work continues.
- **Possible resources**: CPU time, a lock, a worker thread, a connection, or queue capacity.
- **No cycle required**: that separates it from deadlock.
- **Fair lock**: can reduce lock starvation; it is not a strict scheduling guarantee.
- **Prevention**: short critical sections, bounded work, sensible pool sizing, and no dependence on thread priority for correctness.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Starvation happens when a thread or task is able to run in principle but keeps losing access to the resource it needs while other work continues. It can wait for CPU time, a heavily contested lock, a worker in an overloaded pool, or a connection that other tasks repeatedly obtain first.

That differs from deadlock: deadlock has a dependency cycle that stops the involved threads, while starvation is unfair or unbounded delay without needing a cycle. For lock contention, `new ReentrantLock(true)` uses a fair acquisition policy and usually gives the longest-waiting contender preference. I would describe that as reducing starvation, not guaranteeing strict FIFO completion, because scheduling and `tryLock()` have separate behavior. I would also shorten critical sections and inspect queue-wait metrics rather than assume a fairness flag solves every resource bottleneck.

questions.question: What is thread interference and how does it cause problems?
questions.title: Thread Interference in Java
questions.direct_answer: Thread interference is one form of race condition: steps from operations on the same shared data interleave and one operation disturbs another. A common example is a lost update when two threads execute `counter++`. Use an atomic operation or protect the complete read-modify-write with the same lock.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deeper understanding of how operations interleave at the CPU and bytecode level
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming single-statement Java code is always atomic — not knowing that counter-plus-plus is three operations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the exact bytecode-level interleaving that causes a lost update in a counter increment

sections.title: Thread Interference at the Bytecode Level
sections.content:
**Thread interference** happens when operations from different threads overlap on the same mutable state and their individual steps disturb one another.

Consider `counter++`. Its observable job is read the current value, calculate the next value, and store it. Those actions are not one atomic operation. If two threads both read 10, each may store 11, so one update disappears. The exact bytecode or machine instructions are an implementation detail; the safe conclusion is that the Java expression is a compound read-modify-write.

Protect the operation, not just one access. `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` provides an atomic counter update. A `synchronized` block using the same monitor on every access can protect a larger invariant. A `volatile int` makes reads and writes visible, but `counter++` can still lose updates.

sections.title: The Interleaving That Loses an Update
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Thread A
    participant M as Shared count
    participant B as Thread B
    A->>M: read count (10)
    Note over A: computes 11, not stored yet
    B->>M: read count (10)
    B->>M: write 11
    A->>M: write 11
    Note over M: final value 11, one update lost
```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Thread interference|~Operations disturb each other|shared mutable state|overlapping actions|incorrect result possible
blue|Read-modify-write|~Compound operation|counter++ is not atomic|two updates can use one old value|lost update
emerald|Other forms|~Check then act|several related fields|iteration plus mutation|define complete invariant
violet|Fixes|~Remove or coordinate sharing|immutability or confinement|atomic API for one value|same lock for larger invariant

sections.title: Wrong: count++ interleaves across threads
Right: AtomicInteger does the whole step atomically
When Thread Interference Happens
sections.content: Thread interference can occur when operations on shared mutable state overlap without a protocol that protects their full invariant. Examples include read-modify-write, check-then-act, and coordinated changes to several fields. Plain reads and writes have type-specific atomicity rules, but that does not make a compound algorithm atomic; the JLS also permits non-volatile `long` and `double` writes to be treated as two 32-bit writes. Use an atomic operation, the same lock, confinement, immutability, or a suitable concurrent collection method according to the complete operation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming single statements are atomic**: the biggest mistake — thinking `counter++` is safe because it is one line, not realizing the expression is not specified as one atomic action.
- **Synchronizing only one side**: adding `synchronized` to the getter but not the increment does not prevent interference — both need the same lock.
- **Thinking `volatile` fixes interference**: `volatile` ensures visibility but does **not** make compound operations atomic — `volatile int` with `count++` still loses updates.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Thread interference**: operations on shared mutable data interleave and disturb one another.
- **Lost update**: two increments can produce one net change.
- **One line is not one atomic action**: `counter++` is a compound read-modify-write.
- **`volatile` is not enough** for a compound increment.
- **Fix the whole operation** with an atomic method or a common lock.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Thread interference is the concrete overlap that can produce a race condition. Suppose two threads increment the same `int`. Each increment must read a value, calculate the next one, and store it. If both read 10 before either completes, both can store 11 and one update is lost.

The exact number of bytecode or CPU instructions is not the rule to remember; compilers and JVM implementations can differ. The language-level rule is that `counter++` is not an atomic operation. I would use `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` for an independent counter, or one `synchronized` region when the counter changes together with other state. Marking the field `volatile` would make plain reads and writes visible but would not make the read-modify-write indivisible.

questions.question: What is deadlock and what are the four conditions required for it?
questions.title: Deadlock Four Conditions in Java
questions.direct_answer: Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions: Mutual Exclusion (resources are non-shareable), Hold and Wait (holding one resource while waiting for another), No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and Circular Wait (circular chain of waiting threads). Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the formal deadlock conditions — often asked in senior or strong fresher interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing deadlock only as two threads waiting for each other without naming the four Coffman conditions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all four Coffman conditions and explain which one is easiest to break in Java code — typically Circular Wait through lock ordering

sections.title: Deadlock and the Four Coffman Conditions
sections.content:
**Deadlock** is when two or more threads are stuck forever, each holding a lock the other needs.

Think of two cars meeting on a one-lane bridge — neither can pass, and neither will reverse. Computer scientist Edward Coffman listed four conditions that must **all** be true at the same time for deadlock to happen, called the **Coffman conditions**: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait.

The powerful part is that you only need to break **one** of them to make deadlock impossible.

> **Key rule:** in Java code, the easiest condition to break is **Circular Wait** — acquire your `synchronized` locks in one consistent global order (say, by ascending `id`) so a cycle can never form.

The classic Java case: Thread A locks Resource 1 then waits for Resource 2, while Thread B locks Resource 2 then waits for Resource 1. Both wait forever.

sections.title: The Circular Wait That Forms a Deadlock
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR T1[Thread 1
holds Lock A] -->|waits for| LB[Lock B] T2[Thread 2
holds Lock B] -->|waits for| LA[Lock A] LB --> T2 LA --> T1 ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Mutual Exclusion|~Coffman 1|resource non-shareable|one holder at a time|the lock itself
blue|Hold and Wait|~Coffman 2|holds one lock|waits for another|grabs incrementally
emerald|No Preemption|~Coffman 3|cannot force-release|holder keeps it|until done
violet|Circular Wait|~Coffman 4|A waits B, B waits A|the cycle|break this one to prevent

sections.title: Wrong: lock order depends on the arguments
Right: always lock the lower id first
When Deadlock Prevention Matters
sections.content:
You need to prevent deadlock any time your code acquires **more than one lock**. This is critical in fund transfers between accounts (each account is a lock), inventory updates across multiple products, or database code that locks multiple rows.

In Spring `@Transactional` methods that call other services, inconsistent lock orders can deadlock at the database level too. The most practical fix is **lock ordering** — always acquire locks in the same global order, such as by ascending ID. As a safety net, use `tryLock` with a timeout from `ReentrantLock` so a thread can give up instead of waiting forever.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only describing two threads waiting**: saying "A waits for B and B waits for A" without naming the four Coffman conditions loses points in formal interviews.
- **Thinking `synchronized` alone prevents deadlock**: it prevents race conditions, but inconsistent lock order with `synchronized` is exactly what *causes* deadlock.
- **Not knowing which condition to break**: in Java, breaking Circular Wait via lock ordering is the standard solution — many freshers do not know this.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Deadlock**: permanent blocking where threads wait in a cycle for locks held by each other.
- **Mutual Exclusion**: a lock can only be held by one thread at a time.
- **Hold and Wait**: a thread holds one lock while waiting to acquire another.
- **No Preemption**: a lock cannot be forcibly taken — the holder must release it.
- **Circular Wait**: a closed chain of threads each waiting on the next thread's lock.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Deadlock is when two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource the other holds. For deadlock to happen, you need all four Coffman conditions present at the same time. Let me name them. First, Mutual Exclusion — the resource can't be shared, like a synchronized lock that only one thread can hold. Second, Hold and Wait — a thread holds one lock while trying to acquire another. Third, No Preemption — you can't forcibly take a lock away, it has to be released voluntarily. Fourth, Circular Wait — there's a circular chain where thread A waits for thread B's lock, and B waits for A's lock. Here's the key insight: you only need to break one condition to prevent deadlock. In Java code, the easiest one to break is Circular Wait by using lock ordering. That means if you need to lock two accounts, always lock them in ascending ID order. Thread one locks account ten then account twenty. Thread two also locks ten then twenty. Now there's no cycle, no deadlock. Some freshers think synchronized alone prevents deadlock, but that's wrong — deadlock happens when you have multiple synchronized blocks acquired in inconsistent order. The interviewer is testing whether you know the formal conditions, not just the intuitive explanation.

questions.question: What is livelock and how is it different from deadlock?
questions.title: Livelock vs Deadlock in Java
questions.direct_answer: In deadlock, threads cannot progress because they wait in a dependency cycle. In livelock, threads keep changing state or retrying in response to one another but still complete no useful work. Livelock often consumes CPU, but CPU level and Java thread state are symptoms, not definitions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Distinguishing between the two types of stuck conditions — deadlock versus livelock
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing livelock with deadlock or not having a concrete example of livelock
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the classic polite people in a hallway analogy and explain why livelock is harder to detect in production

sections.title: Deadlock vs Livelock: Different Ways to Get Stuck
sections.content:
**Deadlock** and **livelock** both stop useful progress, but for different reasons.

In deadlock, each participant waits for an event that another participant in the same cycle cannot perform—for example, two threads hold one lock each and wait for the other lock. Depending on the primitive, a thread dump may show `BLOCKED`, `WAITING`, or a parked thread.

In livelock, participants are not permanently waiting on that cycle. They keep reacting, retrying, yielding, or releasing resources, but their reactions repeat and no operation finishes. Two retry loops that always collide are a typical example. Livelock may show high CPU when retries spin, or lower CPU when retries include sleeps, so diagnose it by measuring completed work as well as activity.

Break a deadlock with consistent lock ordering or by removing a hold-and-wait cycle. Break a livelock with asymmetric rules, bounded/randomized backoff, or a design that guarantees one participant eventually wins.

sections.title: The Retry Loop That Never Resolves
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Thread grabs first lock] --> B[Tries second lock] B --> C{Got it?} C -- No --> D[Release first lock
and retry] D --> A C -- Yes --> E[Make progress] ```

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Deadlock|~No useful progress|participants wait in a dependency cycle|state depends on primitive|find the cycle
blue|Livelock|~No useful progress|participants keep reacting or retrying|CPU use can vary|measure completions
emerald|Diagnose|~Use evidence|thread dump plus lock graph|throughput and retry count|do not infer from one state
violet|Fixes|~Restore progress|lock ordering for deadlock|break symmetry for livelock|bounded backoff or timeout

sections.title: Deadlock vs Livelock Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | Deadlock | Livelock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thread state | BLOCKED or WAITING | RUNNABLE (actively executing) |
| CPU usage | Zero — threads parked | High — threads spinning |
| Progress | No progress, waiting forever | No progress, but actively trying |
| Detection | Thread dumps show BLOCKED | Hard to detect, appears busy |
| Typical cause | Circular lock acquisition | Collision detection and retry |

sections.title: Livelock: Active but Making No Progress
When Each Problem Occurs
sections.content:
**Deadlock** occurs when acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order — the classic case is two account transfers locking in opposite directions. You will see threads stuck in `BLOCKED` state waiting for synchronized locks or database row locks.

**Livelock** occurs in optimistic retry scenarios where threads detect a conflict and back off, but their retry timing keeps colliding. It is common in lock-free algorithms using compare-and-swap where many threads repeatedly fail the swap and retry. In production, use `jstack` or thread dumps to tell them apart: deadlock shows `BLOCKED` threads with clear lock dependencies, while livelock shows `RUNNABLE` threads with high CPU and no progress.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using the terms interchangeably**: calling every stuck condition "deadlock" misses that livelock is a distinct problem with different symptoms.
- **Not knowing the hallway analogy**: it is the standard explanation interviewers expect — not having it ready looks unprepared.
- **Forgetting CPU usage**: the key differentiator is that livelock burns CPU while deadlock does not — leaving this out misses the practical impact.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Deadlock**: no progress because participants wait in a dependency cycle.
- **Livelock**: participants keep reacting or retrying but complete no useful work.
- **Thread states vary**: deadlock is not always `BLOCKED`, and livelock is not always high-CPU `RUNNABLE`.
- **Deadlock fix**: consistent ordering, timeouts, or remove the cycle.
- **Livelock fix**: break symmetry with bounded/randomized backoff or a winner rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Deadlock means threads cannot continue because they are waiting in a cycle. A simple case is Thread A holding lock 1 while waiting for lock 2, and Thread B holding lock 2 while waiting for lock 1. Livelock means the threads are still taking actions—such as releasing and retrying—but their responses keep colliding, so no request completes.

I would not diagnose the difference from CPU usage or one thread state alone. A monitor deadlock may show `BLOCKED`, while locks built on parking may show `WAITING`; a livelock can spin at high CPU or sleep between retries. I would use a thread dump plus progress metrics. Consistent lock ordering prevents the usual deadlock cycle. Randomized or bounded backoff can break a livelock by stopping both participants from repeating the same timing.

questions.question: What is memory inconsistency and how does the Java Memory Model address it?
questions.title: Memory Inconsistency and Java Memory Model
questions.direct_answer: Memory inconsistency means a thread is allowed to observe stale or unexpectedly ordered effects of another thread because the program has no required happens-before relationship. The Java Memory Model defines the guarantees. A volatile hand-off, release and later acquire of the same monitor, thread start/join, and concurrent utilities can create the needed ordering.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the JMM conceptually — a strong differentiation point for freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the JMM exists or thinking Java memory is always consistent across threads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the key happens-before rules: program order, monitor lock, volatile, thread start and join

sections.title: Memory Inconsistency and the Java Memory Model
sections.content:
A **memory-consistency error** occurs when threads communicate through shared variables without the ordering required by the Java Memory Model. One thread may then observe a stale value or see related writes in an order the programmer did not expect.

The safe model is not 'flush a CPU cache to main memory.' Java deliberately describes this with **happens-before** rules so the guarantee works across processors and JVM implementations. If action A happens-before action B, the effects of A are visible to B and ordered before it.

Examples include unlocking a monitor before another thread later locks the same monitor, writing a volatile variable before another thread reads that write, starting a thread after preparing its input, and returning from `join()` after the joined thread finishes. Use those language guarantees, immutable publication, or `java.util.concurrent` classes instead of relying on timing.

sections.title: Why a Stale Cache Hides a Write
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Thread A writes data"] --> B["A performs a publishing action"]
    B -->|"happens-before"| C["Thread B performs matching action"]
    C --> D["B may safely observe the published data"]
    A -. "no ordering rule" .-> E["B may observe stale or unexpectedly ordered state"]
```

The guarantee comes from the matching synchronization actions—for example, unlock/lock of the same monitor or a volatile publication/read—not from elapsed time.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Memory consistency|~Cross-thread observation without ordering|stale or unexpected state permitted|not merely two caches disagreeing|identify publication protocol
blue|Java Memory Model|~Portable rules|happens-before|synchronization order|does not prescribe physical cache traffic
emerald|Ordering edges|~Examples|same-monitor unlock then lock|volatile publication then observation|start and join rules
violet|Design|~Publish safely|immutability|locks or volatile|concurrent utilities

sections.title: Wrong: a non-volatile flag can be cached or reordered
Right: volatile establishes happens-before
When Memory Visibility Matters
sections.content:
Memory visibility matters in any multi-threaded code where one thread writes and another reads shared state without a lock. The classic case is a flag that signals readiness or shutdown — one thread sets `shouldStop = true`, another checks it in a loop. Without `volatile`, the reader may loop forever on a stale value.

Lazy initialization and publisher-subscriber patterns need the same care: readers must see a fully built object, not a half-published one. The double-checked locking singleton requires `volatile` on the instance field. Any shared state changed without `synchronized` must consider visibility.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reasoning only from CPU caches:** the JMM defines observable ordering across JVM and hardware implementations.
- **Assuming elapsed time publishes a write:** sleeping or waiting longer does not create happens-before.
- **Forgetting monitor identity:** unlock orders a later lock of that same monitor.
- **Using volatile for a multi-step invariant:** a volatile field does not make related updates one transaction.
- **Calling every differing observation a bug in Java:** without the required ordering, the program itself has not established the visibility it expects.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Problem**: a thread may observe stale or unexpectedly ordered effects without proper synchronization.
- **JMM**: defines legal cross-thread observations.
- **Happens-before**: gives visibility and ordering from one action to another.
- **Common edges**: same-monitor unlock/lock, volatile write/read, thread start, and successful join.
- **Do not reason as cache flushing**: code to Java's memory-model rules, not one hardware picture.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Memory inconsistency happens when threads share data but the program has no Java Memory Model rule ordering the writer and reader. A reader may keep seeing an old flag, or it may see a publication flag without safely seeing all the state that was meant to accompany it.

The JMM solves this through happens-before relationships. For example, writes done before releasing a monitor become visible to a thread that later acquires the same monitor. Writes before a volatile publication become visible after another thread observes that volatile write. `Thread.start()` and successful completion observed through `join()` also create ordering. I explain it this way instead of saying Java literally flushes every value to 'main memory,' because the specification promises observable ordering and visibility, not one cache implementation.

familiarity_anchors: two people reading the same page of a book but from different printings
a shared spreadsheet that hasn't synced across devices
two monitors showing different values for the same sensor
speakable_v2.hook: Wall-clock time means nothing for visibility. The Java Memory Model says when one thread's write reaches another.

beats.text: Memory inconsistency is when two threads see different values for the same variable. the program lacks a Java Memory Model ordering rule, while implementations may cache or reorder within that contract. The Java Memory Model defines happens-before rules. They say exactly when one thread's write is visible to another.

CPUs and JVMs reorder and cache values for speed. Without an ordering rule, timing proves nothing. Thread A might write a value, and Thread B might still read the old one. the reader has no happens-before guarantee requiring that observation.

items: Program order: inside one thread, each step happens-before the next.
Monitor lock: a release happens-before the next lock on the same monitor.
Volatile: a volatile write happens-before every later read of it.
Thread start and join: `start` happens-before the new thread's work.

beats.text: Picture a flag set to true at ten o'clock. Another thread reads it a second later. Here's the non-obvious part. The JVM can still return false. Timing alone gives no guarantee. Only `volatile`, `synchronized`, or a thread start creates the real happens-before edge.

items: Syncing the write but not the read still breaks. An unsynced read sees a stale value.
Without `volatile` or `synchronized`, one thread's flag change may never arrive.

speakable_v2.cap: So the Java Memory Model is the contract for visibility. Happens-before is why `volatile` and `synchronized` exist.
